title: Faye and the Ticklish Thimble
markdown:
Faye the ferret had a tail that wiggled like a tiny happy spring. Bumble the moon-moth left trails of sparkly stardust wherever he flittered. They lived in a sewing room that was a rainbow explosion: fluffy fabric scraps like marshmallow mountains, spools of thread in rows like rainbow sweets. Coziest room you ever did see.

But Faye had the so-bores. She had skidded down every fabric slide and zoomed through every thread tunnel. She flopped on polka-dot fluff and sighed a dramatic ferret sigh. “Is this all there is? Just fluff and fuzz and more fluff and fuzz?”

Fluff and fuzz, fluff and fuzz — until, zing, something shiny and silver tumbled off the sewing table. A thimble no bigger than a pinky tip. Clickety-clackety it bounced, and rolled right out the open window.

Faye’s whiskers perked. “An adventure.” Her tail did a wild wiggle-jig. She darted after the glimmer. Bumble, usually shy, perched on a sliver of moonlight, blinked, and whooshed after her. A whisper of moon-dust, tiny fallen stars, drifted down.

The thimble bounced into the orchard. Fat rosy apples dangled. Plump berries hid. Faye wriggled past a towering sunflower and skidded. There: the thimble, stopped at the feet of a very tall, very lumpy scarecrow.

He looked as if he had worn the same patched coat for a million years. His frown was as crooked as tangled thread. He grumbled, pebbles in a tin can. “Aha. Another lost button for my hoard.” A straw-filled hand reached.

“That’s not a button,” Faye squeaked, chest puffed. “That’s a thimble.”

Just then Bumble landed ever so gently on the scarecrow’s pointy hat. Shimmery wings brushed dry scratchy straw.

A-choo.

Not a grumpy sneeze. A tickly, bubbly, giggly sneeze. A-choo. A-choo. A cloud of shimmering dust, moonlight and tickles. The straw rustled happy.

More sparkly dust drifted. The scarecrow chuckled. Then he laughed. He wiggled straw fingers that suddenly did not look so scratchy. “It tickles.” His voice was a happy rumbling drum. He even did a little jig, lumpy arms flailing in a surprisingly funny way.

Faye and Bumble blinked. This scarecrow was not grumpy. He was itchy. And maybe a little lonely, collecting things he thought were lost treasures.

“I’m not grumpy,” he said, frown smoothing into a smile that crinkled his straw face. “I just really like shiny things. They remind me of the stars. That looks like the hat-pin for Lily’s favourite doll. Cottage by the garden fence.”

Faye’s tail thumped the grass. “We can help take it back.”

So they did. Faye nudged the thimble, tail wiggling. Bumble fluttered overhead, a glittering beacon. The scarecrow, who shyly said he was Mr. Pipkin, shuffled behind, lighter than he had been in a long time.

At the cottage a girl named Lily sat with a doll. “My dolly’s best hat is missing its special pin.” Then she saw the thimble — the hat-pin — and her face lit brighter than a thousand fireflies. “Thank you.”

Mr. Pipkin beamed across his whole straw face. Helping felt better than hoarding.

They walked back through apples and berries. Faye’s tail kept the wiggle-jig. Bumble left a little shimmer on Mr. Pipkin’s hat, and the hat, for once, did not sneeze. The sewing room still waited with its fluff and fuzz, fluff and fuzz — and the orchard, just outside the window, waited too.
